account:
Today I reviewed my appointment books and attended morning office business. The builder has arranged an eighteen-hundred inspection of the great hall's new lighting; I approved it yesterday, and the secretary recorded it. The builder says he will meet me shortly beforehand and accompany me inside. As far as I know, its purpose is a lighting inspection; I have no evidence of another purpose.

The unusual business concerns grain and bread. The secretary overheard the builder discussing a grain shortage and seeking the miller's assistance yesterday, with forty-six hay bales mentioned. Neither the quantity nor the circumstances has been verified. The neighbour personally saw the baker give bread to the innkeeper yesterday, heard the innkeeper ask about spare wheat or hay, and heard from freight that they were seeking the miller about arrangements. The neighbour also reports that the baker said yesterday's bread arrangements went smoothly and that fresh bread was being baked today. These reports suggest people are arranging grain supplies and bread distribution, but I do not yet know whether there is a serious shortage or how the builder's request fits in.

I went to the mill for my ten-o'clock grain inspection but could not find the miller. The neighbour likewise got no answer there this morning. My call did not reach him, so I could not inspect stocks with him or verify the reports. I also checked near the bakery oven without finding the baker. Nearby townsfolk repeated an unclear report of a 'bridge_or_port_change' at the bakery involving the baker and neighbour, and said the baker carried a sack of bread. They gave no intelligible details of a bridge or port change, so I do not regard any such change as confirmed.

I am now home at 11:38 for my noon lunch appointment. Next are council letters in the office at thirteen hundred, tea with the neighbour at the dockside cottage at fifteen hundred, office at sixteen-thirty, the great-hall inspection at eighteen hundred, and home at nineteen hundred. The main outstanding question is the actual grain supply and the arrangements involving the miller, builder, baker, innkeeper, and freight.
